title: Google Brings Gemini AI to Chrome on Android for Indian Users
excerpt: The in-browser assistant summarises pages, answers questions about what’s on screen and connects with Google apps — while the new agentic Auto Browse feature arrives restricted to paid subscribers.
body:
• Google has announced that Gemini in Chrome is now available to all Android users in India, bringing its AI browsing assistant directly into the browser — no separate app or tab-switching required.
  • The assistant can summarise lengthy webpages, answer questions about the content on screen, work with Google apps such as Keep and Calendar, and generate or edit images using Nano Banana.
  • Auto Browse, Google's more agentic feature that can carry out multi-step web tasks — booking parking for an event, filling out a long form, ordering groceries — is rolling out on both desktop and Android in India.
  • Caveats for users: Auto Browse is restricted to Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, and Gemini in Chrome on Android is initially available in US and UK English only — with more languages, including Indian ones, planned.

Google is putting Gemini directly inside Chrome for Android users in India, its biggest step yet toward making the browser an AI assistant. Announced this week, the rollout lets Indian users summarise pages, interrogate web content and connect with Google apps without leaving their tab — and the agentic Auto Browse feature arrives in India alongside it.

What Gemini in Chrome does on Android

Gemini in Chrome works within the browser, letting users interact with the webpage they are already on. According to Google, that eliminates the need to leave the current tab or switch between multiple apps. The assistant can summarise long articles, answer questions about the page on screen, and connect with Google services including Keep and Calendar. It also has built-in access to Nano Banana, Google's AI image generation and editing model, so users can customise or generate images while browsing.

The move extends a rollout that began earlier this year. In March, Google expanded Gemini in Chrome to India, New Zealand and Canada beyond the United States, adding support for more than 50 languages — including Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil on desktop, where the assistant appears as a side panel.

Auto Browse: the agentic layer

"The India context India is a natural priority for this kind of rollout: a mobile-first market where Android dominates and Chrome is the default window to the web for hundreds of millions of users."

The headline addition for power users is Auto Browse, Google's more agentic implementation of Gemini in Chrome. Instead of simply answering questions about a webpage, Auto Browse can carry out multi-step tasks on the web: Google's examples include handling jobs such as booking parking for an event, filling out a lengthy form, or ordering groceries.

The feature was released in select global markets in January, but India was excluded. That is now changing — in India, Auto Browse is available on both desktop and Android, although access is restricted to Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers.

Google says the feature has guardrails for sensitive actions. Its models are trained to identify known threats such as prompt injection — a technique that manipulates an AI agent through content on a webpage — and Auto Browse can ask users for confirmation before proceeding with certain sensitive tasks.

The India context

India is a natural priority for this kind of rollout: a mobile-first market where Android dominates and Chrome is the default window to the web for hundreds of millions of users. But the Android launch starts with a limitation — it is initially available in US and UK English only, with more languages planned over time. By comparison, the desktop version already works in eight Indian languages, so the language gap on Android is a clear next step for Google to close.

The launch also lands in a competitive moment. AI assistants are racing to live where users already are — inside the browser — rather than as standalone destinations. Google's advantage is distribution: Chrome's installed base means Gemini's browsing features reach users without a download or a new habit.

Impact and analysis

For Google, the Android expansion matters because so much daily work begins on a phone. Moving from assistance that answers questions to assistance that completes tasks — even behind a paid tier — is the direction the whole industry is heading, and India is now one of the testing grounds.

The subscription restriction on Auto Browse is the commercial tell. Google will give away summarisation to everyone, but the genuinely agentic work — tasks that replace human clicks — sits behind the paywall. Expect competitors to contest that line as they price their own agents.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the rollout is doubly relevant: family members in India get the same AI-assisted browsing that users in the US have had, and the desktop version's eight Indian-language support means parents who prefer Hindi or Tamil can use it. NRIs travelling to India will also find their Android phones behaving consistently across borders.

What's next

Watch for the Android language expansion — Indian-language support is the obvious gap, given it already exists on desktop — and for Google to broaden the set of tasks Auto Browse can reliably complete. The company has not published a full list of supported tasks, so early users will be the real testers of how much agency the feature actually delivers.
